title: The strict practices
hookLine: rag robes, alms food, living in the forest: the Buddha tells Kassapa he is old and may let them go, and Kassapa explains why he keeps them (SN 16.5)

cards: The robes are heavy now. That's the first thing the Buddha says in this short discourse. Kassapa has grown old, and the hempen rag robes he's worn so long hang heavy on him.
So the Buddha makes a kind offer: you're old, Kassapa. Wear the robes householders give you, accept meals when people invite you, and live near me instead of out in the forest.
Nobody would blame him; his teacher is giving permission. And Kassapa, politely, says no.

teach.b: First, what he keeps. Kassapa lists his way of life: a long time in the forest, eating only alms food, wearing rag robes, keeping only the robes he needs, wanting little, content, secluded, putting in effort.
And he praises these things to others too.
Later tradition gathers practices like these under one name, dhutanga. Second, the name.
In the Path of Purification, Buddhaghosa's long handbook, they're explained as practices of a monk who has shaken off the defilements. They're not required of anyone.
They're chosen, on top of the ordinary rules, by those who want a sharper, simpler life. Third, his reasons. The Buddha asks why he keeps them, and Kassapa gives two.

teach.h: A PLEASANT LIFE, HERE AND NOW.
teach.b: One: they make a pleasant life for him, here and now. He isn't suffering through them; he likes living this way.
Two: compassion for those who come later. He hopes people in the future will say, the Buddha's disciples lived like this, and take heart, and try it too.
Fourth, the answer. The Buddha says: good, good, Kassapa. You're practicing for the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world.
So an old man keeps carrying heavy robes, not to prove anything, but so someone he'll never meet can see the path is still walked.

how: In the Thai forest tradition and other Theravada communities, some monks take up dhutanga practices for a time or for life, such as eating one meal a day from the alms round or living in the forest, while others keep only the ordinary rules.

games.q: you're Kassapa, old, and your teacher kindly offers to let you live an easier life. what do you do?
o: keep the strict practices, and explain why.
accept, but keep one practice in secret.
games.why: he keeps them, for his own pleasant life and as an example for those to come, and the Buddha approves.

practice: Think of one small, plain habit you keep or once kept: a walk without the phone, tea without a screen, one meal eaten slowly.

Ask Kassapa's two questions about it: does it make this life a little more pleasant, here and now, and who might see it, a child, a roommate, a friend, and quietly take it up? No big answer is needed; then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Dhutanga. Simple, strict practices, like forest living, alms food and rag robes, taken up by choice; Kassapa keeps them into old age. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dhutanga: the practices of one who shakes off defilements, in the Path of Purification's explanation.

carryVoice: Your line: for those to come. A simple life can be a gift to people you'll never meet. Day seven hundred forty-one, done.
